note: Golden refusal vectors for the recipient-resolution contract. ONE file, replayed by rine-core/test/recipient-refusal-golden.test.ts (ci.sh stage 11) and rine-sdk/tests/contract/test_recipient_refusal_golden.py (ci.sh stage 4). Two copies of this file is the failure the gate exists to prevent. `vectors` and `excluded` are pure input -> composed sentence: no HTTP, no client, no server. `by_id_disclosure` and `by_id_substitution` are the two exceptions and each says why in its own note — the by-id disclosure rule is a mapping from a STATUS to a sentence and the by-id substitution rule from a BODY to a typed raise, and no arrangement of a roster and a spelling can express either. Regenerate with RINE_REFUSAL_REGEN=1 and run BOTH replays — each writes only its own stack's fields. Vector INPUTS are ASCII; the expected sentences carry whatever bytes the product composes, including the em dash and the ellipsis of the overflow row, which are load-bearing.

slots.bare_recipient_group: recipientGroupForBareName(candidates, spelling) / recipient_group_for_bare_name(...), the refusal it raises
slots.bare_agent_collision: refuseIfABareAgentName(agents, spelling) / refuse_if_a_bare_agent_name(...), the refusal it raises; null when it raises none
slots.compose_bare: the composer with a lead and nothing else
slots.compose_next_step_no_roster: the composer with a lead and a next step
slots.compose_next_step_under_roster: the composer with a lead, a roster AND a next step
slots.compose_next_step_empty_roster: the composer with a lead, an EMPTY roster and a next step
slots.invalid_agent_identifier: invalidAgentIdentifierRefusal(spelling) / invalid_agent_identifier(...) — the sentence resolveToUuid / resolve_to_uuid_{sync,async} raises for a spelling that is neither a UUID nor a handle. One raise site per stack, so the sentence can be compared at all: the resolver is async and reaches WebFinger on its other arm, which is how a one-byte divergence (terminated on TS, unterminated on Python) hides from every per-stack suite while all of them read green. Each stack also asserts locally that its resolver raises exactly this.
slots.join_bare_name: bareNameJoinRefusal(spelling) / bare_name_join_refusal(...) — first of the two composers JOIN_TAKES_A_HANDLE_OR_AN_ID is spliced into. The constant is pinned as a CONSTANT by the backend gate JOIN_REFUSAL_TWIN_SENTENCES; that gate reads two module sources and cannot see what a composer does with the string, which is the hole these two slots close.
slots.join_unresolved_handle: unresolvedHandleJoinRefusal(spelling, unread) / unresolved_handle_join_refusal(...) — the other composer JOIN_TAKES_A_HANDLE_OR_AN_ID is spliced into. `unread` picks which middle sentence is spliced in (0 = the directory ran to the end), so both arms are replayed and the constant is proven to survive in each.
slots.not_a_conversation_uuid: notAConversationUuidRefusal(spelling, THREAD_REF_SURFACES[surface]) / not_a_conversation_uuid(...) — the surface-parameterised composer. The vector names its `surface` because TypeScript parameterises the two parameter spellings and Python hardcodes the tool ones; the Python replay asserts the vector names the surface it implements rather than composing a sentence for a surface it has never had.

by_id_disclosure.note: 🔴 The by-id disclosure rule, and the ONE section of this file that is not pure input → sentence. `GET /groups/{id}` 404s an id no group carries and 403s one carried by a group of an org this caller is neither owner of nor seated in, and the two must be indistinguishable: telling them apart would tell a stranger which unknown ids EXIST, which is the non-member lookup the protocol refuses to add. That rule is a mapping from a STATUS to a sentence, so no arrangement of a roster and a spelling can express it — each replay drives its own seated resolver (resolveGroup / RineSyncClient.resolve_group) against a stub transport instead. It is here and not only in each stack's own suite because both stacks already guard it SEPARATELY (rine-core/test/resolve-group-handle.test.ts and rine-sdk/tests/contract/test_recipient_parity.py::TestResolveGroup) and neither of those compares the two stacks' BYTES — which is the class of hole a one-byte divergence in invalidAgentIdentifierRefusal hides in while every suite reads green. `expected` is written by the Python replay alone, exactly as it is for the shared vectors. `propagated` is the bound the rule needs and not decoration: a blanket catch would compose a roster refusal for an outage and send a caller off to re-spell a perfectly good id, so a status outside `indistinguishable` must escape as itself. 429 is deliberately not among them — the transport retries it with backoff, and the wait is the transport's business rather than the resolver's.

by_id_substitution.note: 🔴 The by-id substitution rule — the UUID rung checks the row it got back, and this is the second section of this file that is DRIVEN rather than composed. The rung reads a row and five further surfaces route through it, so a body naming another group would make every downstream verb act on that group while the caller believed it had addressed its own. The rule is a mapping from a BODY to a raise, which no arrangement of a roster and a spelling can express, so each replay drives its own seated resolver (resolveGroup / RineSyncClient.resolve_group) against a stub transport. Three claims per vector, and the last two are the contract: the sentence is byte-identical across the stacks, the raise is TYPED and both stacks name the same type, and the roster is never bought — a server fault surfaces as a server fault, never as a missing group. The `answered` row is what `GET /groups/{id}` replies with; `roster` is what `GET /groups` would have said had anything asked it, which is exactly what must not happen. 🔴 The third vector is the one that would go unnoticed without a shared vector: a group id is a JSON string or it is absent, because `String(x)` and `str(x)` agree on strings and on nothing else (`false`/`False`, `[object Object]`/`{}`), so a body whose `id` is a number, a boolean or an object names NO group on both stacks rather than being rendered — and the sentence says so instead of leaving a blank before the full stop. `expected` is written by the Python replay alone, as it is everywhere else in this file.

excluded.reason: Vectors whose two stacks genuinely disagree. They are carried here, not deleted: each replay asserts its OWN stack's recorded string, so the divergence is PINNED rather than absent — a stack that changes one of these fails, and the day both agree the vector moves into the shared set. Unifying the two stacks to make one of these pass is a product change, not a fixture change.

vectors.divergence: Rule 4 says exactly one trailing '.'. Python's composer terminates every part it is handed (`_terminated`: the part unchanged when it already ends in a stop, otherwise one appended); TypeScript's `joinSentences` normalises only the SEAM between two sentences and leaves the last one exactly as the lead wrote it. So a lead that carries no full stop and has nothing appended to it comes back unterminated on TypeScript and terminated on Python. Unreachable through any shipped call site today — every shipped TypeScript lead either ends in a period or is followed by a roster — which is why no existing test moves. Closing it is a product change, not a fixture change.

vectors.divergence: The same rule-4 gap, on the other tail: Python's composer terminates the next step (`_terminated`, `_group_ref.py`), TypeScript's `joinSentences` leaves the last sentence exactly as it was handed. 🔴 The shipped bytes agree, but NOT because the two callers agree — they agree by two different mechanisms. The earlier reading of this vector, that *'the one shipped caller passes a next step that already ends in a period'*, was true only of TypeScript: `refuseIfABareAgentName` does end its next step in a period, so its non-termination is invisible; `refuse_if_a_bare_agent_name` passes an UNTERMINATED next step and the composer adds the stop. The two callers also split the sentence differently — TypeScript carries 'To message that agent…' in the next step, Python carries it in the lead — so any new caller that hands either stack the other's shape gets the other's tail.

vectors.divergence: Rule 3 fires on different inputs. Python suppresses the next step whenever candidates were PASSED (`candidates is not None`), so an empty roster suppresses it; TypeScript suppresses only when the rendered rows are non-empty (`candidates.rows !== ""`), so an empty roster prints the roster's empty-org sentence AND the next step. Unreachable today: no shipped refusal passes both a roster and a next step. It is the first thing a surface migrating onto these shared composers would hit, because 'there are none, here is how to find one' is the obvious shape for a surface to want.

Python folds 'Straße' onto 'strasse' and refuses; TypeScript lower-cases it to 'straße', matches no agent, and lets the reference through to the group ladder.
